key_concept: In the taxonomic hierarchy, a genus is a group of closely related species that share many common characters but differ from species of other genera.
steps: Recall the taxonomic hierarchy in ascending order: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom.
Each higher category is a group of closely related members of the category just below it.
The category just below genus is species, so a genus is a group of closely related species. Example: the genus *Panthera* includes lion (*P. leo*), tiger (*P. tigris*) and leopard (*P. pardus*).
A group of closely related genera forms a family. A group of closely related families forms an order, not a genus.
An individual organism is not a taxonomic category. A population is a group of interbreeding individuals of one species, so it is not a genus either.
Therefore option (3) is correct, which matches the NTA key.
final_answer: Option (3): a group of closely related species
why_not_others: Option (4) describes an order, because related families group into an order. Options (1) and (2) describe an individual and a population, which lie below or within a single species and are not taxonomic ranks.
common_trap: Students mix up the direction of the hierarchy and pick 'closely related families', which actually describes an order.
time_saving_tip: Remember that each rank is a group of the rank immediately below it. Genus sits just above species, so pick the option with 'species'.
